passage: So, Jomon, you asked on the way home why I waved you off at the canteen counter. This is Chinmay, owning up. That hand thing, the quick flick like shoo, I did it because the queue was crushing me and you were right at my shoulder, and I felt I couldn't breathe. It meant give me air. Not go away. But I saw your face drop, and you went and sat with Anoop without a word. At home my Ammamma does that same flick at the vegetable seller to mean not now, and nobody minds. In your house I think it's rude, right? So I should have said it in words, something like, "Sorry, I'm a bit squashed, give me a second?" I'm saying it now, late. Save me a seat tomorrow?

qa.q: Where did Chinmay wave Jomon off?
qa.a: At the canteen counter.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling in the queue?
qa.a: Chinmay felt crushed and breathless and needed air, not annoyed with Jomon.

qa.q: What could Chinmay have said with the wave to avoid shaming Jomon?
qa.a: A few words like 'Sorry, I'm a bit squashed, give me a second?' to show it meant space, not rejection.

qa.q: How did Jomon seem to take the wave?
qa.a: Jomon's face dropped and Jomon went to sit with Anoop without a word, likely feeling hurt and brushed off.

grounding: It illustrates a hand wave meaning give me air being read as go away, with family habits differing on bluntness and words clarifying it.

subtype: Palm out as boundary in arguments [Regulating]
passage: I'm Maria, their cousin, and I was staying with them for Onam when it happened. Irawati was in the middle of a rant at Joseph about him using her charger again, hands flying, voice climbing. Joseph suddenly put his palm up, flat, right in front of her face. Irawati stopped, but her eyes went narrow. "Did you just palm me? Like I'm a dog?" I couldn't tell what Joseph meant; he just stood there with his hand up. Then he lowered it and said, "Sorry. I meant give me a second. You're right about the charger. I just couldn't think with the shouting." Irawati was still annoyed, but her shoulders came down. "Then say that, not the hand." He nodded, handed her the charger, and said, "Give me a second, please." They both laughed.

qa.q: What had Joseph been using again?
qa.a: Irawati's charger.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when her eyes went narrow?
qa.a: Irawati felt insulted and dismissed, reading the flat palm as being shut up rudely.

qa.q: What kept the respect intact after the palm?
qa.a: Joseph lowered his hand, apologised, agreed about the charger and put his need into words: 'Give me a second.'

qa.q: How did Joseph see his own raised palm?
qa.a: To Joseph it meant 'give me a second': he needed a pause to think through the shouting, not to dismiss Irawati.

grounding: It shows a teenager raising a palm to pause a sibling's rant, the gesture reading as dismissive, and a few words restoring respect, as seen by a cousin.

passage:
Field trip note, bird walk at the lake, Saturday
On the embankment, when Ramesh asked where the kingfisher was, Aparna, who moved here from Manila last year, pushed her lips out towards the reeds. Ramesh thought she was pulling a face at him and said, "What? Just tell me." Aparna looked embarrassed. She explained that at home people often point with their lips, and pointing a finger at people can feel rude to some. Ramesh then admitted he'd been jabbing his finger at every bird and at a couple of fishermen too. Neither style told us where the bird actually was, so I suggested pairing any point with words: "Left of the broken post, on the lowest reed." Ramesh tried it, and the whole group found the kingfisher within seconds. Next step: before our next trip, I will ask students to share how pointing works in their families.

qa.q: Which bird was Ramesh looking for?
qa.a: The kingfisher.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling after Ramesh said "What? Just tell me"?
qa.a: Aparna felt embarrassed, because her lip point had been read as pulling a face.

qa.q: Why did pairing the point with words work?
qa.a: Words like 'left of the broken post' don't depend on anyone's pointing style, so everyone could check and find the bird 👍

qa.q: How did Ramesh first read Aparna's lip pointing?
qa.a: He thought she was making a face at him, not showing where the bird was.

grounding: It illustrates pointing styles differing by region, a lip point being misread, and words plus checking making a gesture clear, as noted by a trip leader.

passage:
Saturday night
Irawati says I nearly knocked the chai off the table today. I was telling her about the last over of the gully match: how the ball came at me like a bullet (arm whoosh), how I dived (whole body sideways onto the sofa), how it stuck in my fingertips (hand up, frozen, dramatic pause). She laughed so hard she snorted.
Then she said something odd: "Last week when you told me about the maths test, your hands stayed in your pockets." She's right. I told that story in about four words, hands dead. I was tired and didn't want to talk about it.
Funny that my hands show how I feel before I say it. Nani says everyone in our family talks with their hands, but my cousin in Delhi barely moves his, even when he's thrilled. So small hands don't always mean sad.
Yash

qa.q: What did Yash nearly knock off the table?
qa.a: The chai.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling while telling the story of the last over?
qa.a: Yash felt excited and thrilled, shown by the whooshing arm, the sideways dive onto the sofa and the frozen, dramatic pause 😄

qa.q: Why should Yash be careful about reading small gestures as sadness?
qa.a: Culture and family shape gesture size, like the cousin who barely moves even when thrilled, so small gestures aren't proof of sadness.

qa.q: How did Irawati read Yash's hands?
qa.a: Irawati noticed big gestures with the exciting match story and still hands with the maths test, and pointed out the difference.

grounding: It shows a teenager's sweeping storytelling gestures signalling excitement, very small ones going with tiredness, and family style shaping gesture size.

passage:
Mentor's note, mock interviews for the science scholarship
Vijay came in with his shoulders curled and his eyes on the floor. Before he spoke, I asked him to stand, plant both feet, let his shoulders drop and take one slow breath. His voice was steadier after that, and his answer on the water-filter project was clear, because he knew every step he had built. Saurabh, next, had clearly watched a video about power poses: he stood with hands on hips, chest out, and held it before starting. He looked confident, but when I asked how his circuit worked, he lost his thread. Afterwards Saurabh laughed and said the pose "didn't work". I told them both the same thing: standing tall can settle nerves for a minute, but knowing your work is what carries an interview. Next step: Saurabh will walk me through his circuit on Thursday; Vijay will practise the breath at the door.

qa.q: Which project did Vijay explain clearly?
qa.a: The water-filter project.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he came in with curled shoulders?
qa.a: Vijay seemed nervous and unsure, eyes on the floor, until the breath and posture settled him.

qa.q: What does the mentor's plan show about confidence?
qa.a: It pairs a simple posture and breath to settle nerves with real preparation, like Saurabh walking through the circuit, because a pose can't replace knowing the work.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt when he lost his thread?
qa.a: Saurabh probably felt embarrassed, having expected the pose to carry him, though he laughed it off.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager using posture and a breath to calm interview nerves, and preparation, not a power pose, supplying real confidence.

subtype: Slumping and crossing arms as protection [Regulating]
passage: The courtyard of the old house in Kallur was full of relatives for the land meeting, and the uncles' voices kept rising. Sunaina sat on the edge of the charpai, hunched forward, arms crossed tight over her chest, chin tucked down. Gopika Mami, passing with a tray of tea, frowned. "Sit up properly, Sunaina. The elders will think you're sulking." Sunaina straightened for a moment, then curled back in as Periappa slammed his hand on the table. Later, when the relatives had gone, Mami found her behind the cowshed. This time she didn't scold. "You looked like you were trying to disappear in there. Were you cold, or was it the shouting?" Sunaina kept her arms crossed. "The shouting. When they get loud like that, I feel small again." Mami sat down beside her on the step. "Tell me about it."

qa.q: What were the relatives gathered for?
qa.a: The land meeting.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling when she curled back in?
qa.a: Sunaina felt frightened and small, with the raised voices and slammed hand making her want to disappear.

qa.q: What changed when Mami found Sunaina behind the cowshed?
qa.a: She asked whether it was the cold or the shouting instead of scolding, then sat down and invited Sunaina to talk.

qa.q: How did Gopika Mami first read Sunaina's posture?
qa.a: She read it as sulking or rudeness in front of the elders and told her to sit up.

grounding: It shows a teenager hunching and crossing her arms to feel smaller and safer in a tense family gathering, and an adult moving from scolding to asking.

passage: Mridul, you keep asking why I didn't dance at the fest when you've seen me dance at my cousin's baraat. Okay, here's Kiran's full explanation, one time only. At the baraat it was dhol, dust, my Tauji's terrible bhangra, and all my cousins pulling me in. Nobody filmed me, nobody cared if I was good. I danced for two hours and felt I belonged to every person on that road. The fest was different. Some seniors said the dance team was "a girls' thing" and started calling the boys who joined silly names. Nobody forced me out, but it didn't feel like choosing either. So I sat out. And I hated sitting out. Next year, if you join with me, I'll do it. Deal? It's my dancing. It's not theirs to decide.

qa.q: How long did Kiran dance at the baraat?
qa.a: For two hours.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while dancing at the baraat?
qa.a: Kiran felt joyful and part of the whole family, free because nobody was filming or judging.

qa.q: What turned dancing from joy into something Kiran avoided at the fest?
qa.a: The seniors' teasing about gender and the names they called the boys, which made joining feel risky rather than a free choice.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel about Kiran's "Deal?"
qa.a: Mridul may feel trusted and glad to help, since joining together could make dancing feel like Kiran's own choice again.

grounding: It illustrates dance as joy and belonging at a family baraat, and gender-based teasing turning it into something avoided, with choice at the centre.

subtype: Walking away as boundary or avoidance [Mismatch]
passage:

Gurleen: I know. sorry
Devika: so what, you don't care?
Gurleen: I do. that's why I left. I was about to say something really mean about your mum's rule and I didn't want to
Devika: it felt like you were running away
Gurleen: I get that. I should've said "I need a break, I'll come back"
Devika: yeah that would've been less 😠
Gurleen: I need a break. I'll come back. is 6 ok? at the park?
Devika: ...ok. 6
Gurleen: and I'm not running away. I just didn't want to hurt you
Devika: 🤍 ok

qa.q: What time and place did Gurleen suggest for meeting?
qa.a: 6, at the park.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when Gurleen walked off?
qa.a: Devika felt hurt and abandoned, reading the walk-off as not caring or running away.

qa.q: What would have made the meaning clear in the moment?
qa.a: Saying 'I need a break, I'll come back' and giving a time, as Gurleen later did with 6 at the park.

qa.q: How did Gurleen see the walk-off?
qa.a: Gurleen saw it as a way to stop before saying something mean about Devika's mum's rule, to avoid hurting Devika.

grounding: It shows walking away from a hard talk read as avoidance, and 'I need a break, I'll come back' making it clear de-escalation that keeps trust.

passage:
Friday: After dance practice, Rohit, a senior, grabbed Binita's phone and found the clip of her tripping on stage. "You don't mind if I post this, right?" Binita's mouth opened, but nothing came out. Her legs wouldn't move. He laughed, said, "Silence means yes," and posted it.
Saturday: Binita told Devika, voice shaking. "I didn't say no. I just stood there." Devika held her hand. "Freezing isn't saying yes. Your body got scared. Let's tell your mum now." They went straight to Binita's home, and her mother listened to all of it, said, "This is not your fault," and emailed the school counsellor and the dance teacher that afternoon.
Monday: The counsellor met Binita first thing, and the clip was taken down by lunch. Rohit was spoken to. In the corridor, Binita still felt her legs go stiff, but now she knew what it meant.

qa.q: What was on the clip Rohit posted?
qa.a: Binita tripping on stage.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when her legs wouldn't move?
qa.a: Binita was frightened and overwhelmed, frozen so that speaking was impossible; it was not agreement.

qa.q: Which steps put things right?
qa.a: Telling Devika, then telling Binita's mother the same day, who said it wasn't Binita's fault and emailed the counsellor and dance teacher; the clip was down by Monday lunch.

qa.q: How did Devika see Binita's silence?
qa.a: Devika saw it as a fear response, not a yes, and said so before helping Binita tell an adult.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager freezing when pressured, the stillness wrongly taken as a yes, and a friend and parent treating freezing as fear, not consent.
